pattern_title: GA inpatient spend is concentrated in a narrow atrial fibrillation and embolism case mix
pattern_description: GA spend growth is heavily concentrated in a narrow set of inpatient cases, led by atrial fibrillation ablation episodes and supported by pulmonary embolism, UTI, and neurologic admissions. The main driver is higher admissions, with several high-cost episodes also showing higher paid per admit. This is a focused clinical management issue rather than a broad statewide trend.

claims.summary: GA atrial fibrillation ablation tied to paroxysmal atrial fibrillation added about $2.6M from 47 more admissions and about $2.5K higher paid per admit. GA atrial fibrillation ablation tied to other persistent atrial fibrillation added about $1.9M from 33 more admissions and about $7.9K higher paid per admit. GA UTI admissions added about $819K from 70 more admissions with about $1.4K higher paid per admit. GA neurologic post-stroke cases added about $1.8M across two diagnosis variants.

pattern_title: Authorization and facility mapping issues are masking true spend in GA, CA, and CT
pattern_description: A meaningful share of reported increase is tied to authorization-code movement and facility records that are not mapped to a facility type. In GA this includes AUTH_CODE_DISTRIBUTION changes, and separate Not Mapped facility spikes appear in GA, CA, and CT. These issues can distort authorization performance, site-of-care reporting, and provider comparisons, so they should be corrected before pricing or policy action.

claims.summary: GA AUTH_CODE_DISTRIBUTION shifts account for about $4.2M, led by Aftercare with CC/MCC at about $2.3M and Kidney and Urinary Tract Infections without MCC at about $1.9M. Not Mapped facility activity adds about $1.8M across GA, CA, and CT. GA Not Mapped facility growth alone added about $1.0M, mostly in Degenerative Nervous System Disorders without MCC. CA and CT also show Not Mapped facility growth, indicating the classification issue is not isolated to GA.

pattern_title: GA authorized acute hospital spend is rising from both more admissions and higher episode cost
pattern_description: In GA PPO Local acute hospitals, authorized inpatient growth is coming from both more admissions and higher episode cost. Atrial fibrillation ablation is the largest driver, with additional pressure from aftercare, pulmonary embolism, UTI, and neurologic admissions. This is not a volume-only issue, so utilization management and reimbursement levers both matter.

claims.summary: GA authorized atrial fibrillation ablation added about $1.6M from 33 more admissions and about $1.9K higher paid per admit. GA authorized UTI acute admissions added about $537K from 76 more admissions and were largely volume-driven. GA authorized aftercare acute admissions added about $445K with paid per admit up about $6.5K. GA authorized pulmonary embolism and neurologic acute admissions added about $705K from 61 more admissions combined.

pattern_title: Physical Rehab growth is becoming a provider and post-acute economics issue in GA, CA, and OH
pattern_description: Physical Rehab spend is rising across GA, CA, and OH PPO Local, with the heaviest concentration in GA and visible provider concentration at GLANCY REHABILITATION CENTER. Growth is tied to aftercare and neurologic rehab cases, and GA also shows rare high-cost rehab episodes layered on top of broader rehab utilization. This points to a post-acute provider economics and admission management opportunity rather than a single isolated claim issue.

claims.summary: GA Physical Rehab mixed pressure added about $1.5M, led by Degenerative Nervous System Disorders without MCC at about $882K and Aftercare with CC/MCC at about $622K. CA Physical Rehab added about $658K from 7 more Aftercare with CC/MCC admissions and about $12.9K higher paid per admit. OH Physical Rehab utilization added about $352K from 16 more Aftercare with CC/MCC admissions. GLANCY REHABILITATION CENTER added about $346K from 11 more rehab admissions, and GA rare rehab cases added another about $675K.

pattern_title: CA acute hospital costs are concentrated in authorized atrial fibrillation ablation and select provider exposure
pattern_description: CA PPO Local acute hospital costs are rising through both utilization and higher paid per admit, led by atrial fibrillation ablation and smaller UTI growth. The increase is concentrated enough to surface provider exposure at ST. JOSEPH'S HOSPITAL AND MEDICAL CENTER, including a small number of very high paid admissions. This calls for a combined contract and authorization review in CA acute settings.

pattern_title: Smaller-market authorized acute hospital growth is emerging across NH, NY, CA, OH, and PA
pattern_description: Outside the larger GA and OH acute hospital patterns, a second tier of authorized acute hospital growth is emerging across NH, NY, CA, OH, and PA. Some of this is straightforward admission growth in pulmonary embolism, UTI, and neurologic stays, but NH and NY also show small-volume atrial fibrillation ablation cases with unusually high paid per admit. Because these markets are low-volume and dispersed, the right action is targeted case and provider intervention before the pattern scales.

pattern_title: OH acute hospital spend shows meaningful authorized unit-cost pressure
pattern_description: OH PPO Local acute hospital spend is rising mainly in authorized acute hospital cases, led by atrial fibrillation ablation and UTI admissions. Unlike the broader multi-state emergence pattern, OH already shows meaningful paid-per-admit escalation, and a very small number of ST. JOSEPH'S HOSPITAL AND MEDICAL CENTER cases are extremely expensive. This makes OH a discrete reimbursement and UM priority.

pattern_title: Rare high-cost inpatient outliers need case-level review, not broad policy changes
pattern_description: A separate set of rare, very expensive inpatient cases is appearing across CA, CT, NH, OH, and GA. These include tracheostomy with prolonged ventilation, lung transplant complications, transplant aftercare, severe trauma, sepsis, pneumonia, and respiratory infection cases, usually as one-off admissions. They are too episodic to support broad policy changes, but they do warrant catastrophic case management, coding confirmation, and individual payment review.
